The lure of paying tribute to Sheryl Crow in speech and song brought out the big guns at an event honoring the singer-songwriter in Nashville Monday night, as Olivia Rodrigo , Chris Stapleton , Jason Isbell, Lauren Daigle, Eric Church and Melissa Etheridge all turned out to turn in stellar covers of Crow’s songs as part of the intimate, invite-only dinner held at BMI ‘s Nashville headquarters.
Crow was receiving the BMI Troubadour Award, typically given to artists who fall into the realms of Americana and/or rootsy rock ‘n’ roll, with previous honorees ranging from John Fogerty to Lucinda Williams. As perhaps the biggest non-country music star living and working in Nashville, Crow was a shoo-in to be selected for that honor, with a guest list befitting her stature and a mini-tribute concert that won’t soon be forgotten by the couple hundred industry guests.
All of the guests sang backed by a house band of Music City stalwarts, Rodrigo was the biggest surprise of the night, having flown in to sing “Strong Enough” in Crow’s honor. Other performances included Isbell kicking off the evening’s performances with “Run Baby Run,” followed by Etheridge singing “If It Makes You Happy,” Daigle doing “Every Day Is a Winding Road,” Eric Church performing “Leaving Las Vegas” and Stapleton tearing into “I Shall Believe.”
Rodrigo prefaced her performance with an anecdote illustrating Crow’s largess. “I just firstly wanted to say what an honor it is to be here tonight celebrating someone incredible,” she said. “Obviously Sheryl is the most magnificent singer-songwriter artist ever, but what inspires me the most about you is your heart and your kindness and your generosity. I’m sure so many people in here have stories like this, but I was thinking about it on the way over. The first time I ever met Sheryl, we were playing at the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame together. We were singing ‘Happy’ with the guitar, and I was playing one of the guitars that the crew gave me, and I was like, ‘This guitar’s awesome. I love it. She goes, ‘Oh, do you want it?’ And I was like, ‘Sure. I’m not gonna take Sheryl Crow’s guitar. And wouldn’t you know it, the next day, I woke up and I got a package and it was Sheryl Crow’s guitar. And I just think that it’s my most prized possession.”
In her acceptance speech wrapping up the night, Crow said, “I tell my bandmates this all the time, but I do feel like this most spoiled, um, let’s just say, legacy artist … as opposed to, like, old lady on the stage. I keep saying to the Grammys, I’m like, ‘You give out Best New. How come you can’t give out Best Old?'”
The night also included video testimonials recorded for the event by the Chicks, Brandi Carlile and other stars. It also featured a lengthy personal speech from someone who is not often in the spotlight, her longtime co-writer and studio guitarist, Jeff Trott, who recalled canceling his agreement to join the Wallflowers when Crow called him and said she wanted him to come in and record songs for her second album that they’d written months earlier and he figured had been abandoned — soon-to-be classics like “If It Makes You Happy” — a change in plans he felt bashful about, as far as leaving the Wallflowers in the lurch, but one he hasn’t regretted, given their 30 subsequent years of constant collaboration. Crow looked back to her family origins and musical upraising. “My mom and dad were both musicians, and they were always playing music on our Magnavox, all the greats, and there was always a great presence of music in my household. And I still consider myself a student of songwriting, and I don’t ever want to think that I know what I’m doing because I think crafting sometimes can get in the way of just being lucky to be in the room when something divine happens. And that literally for me is how I experience my maker — either in the woods or when some incredible melody or words comes and I go, ‘Wow, I wonder where that came from. Thank you, Jesus. Thank you, Lord. Thank you, God. Thank you, universe. Whoever’s doing it, thank you for letting me be a steward of it.’
“I’ve had the really good fortune of having a lot of mentors along the way, between Willie Nelson and Kris Kristofferson and Bob Dylan and Emmylou (Harris), who all let me stand in their orbit and just pick up on their greatness. Especially when I was down and struggling, I had Don Henley and Stevie Nicks, who not only inspired me, but they sort of helped me figure out who I was along the way. And I also have had the good fortune of writing with Chris Stapleton. And hear me when I say, when you work with the greats, it leaves an impact on you, and it makes you want to keep going in search of your best work. And I do feel like… I’m 65, and I feel like my best work is in front of me.”
Crow continued, “I do want to say to young artists, I mean, all the artists that were up here tonight, they make me want to be better. They make me wanna keep going. They make me want to keep writing. I know I got to see young Jesse Welles over there, who I literally attacked on the side of the stage …It’s just the songwriting that’s happening right now, and people who are really willing to help all of us find ourselves in music. It can’t be underestimated — and fuck AI. Sorry, but it will never feel and, also, it will never play live.
“I know we’re all thinking of Dolly, and we’re all feeling her in our hearts. I can’t tell you the many conversations I have with people every day who feel like they have lost a bit of her. And we’re all entertainers, but when you consider how to leave the world a better place than how you found it like she did, a song can be such a healer. It can make a kid feel seen, which is the real reason my mom got into music, is (knowing) that I was a kid that came with a melancholy (appreciation) when James Taylor talked about ‘Fire and Rain’ — I was pretty sure that was me. And that’s what music does. It finds you and it makes you feel like you’re not alone.”
Crow became tearful as she further discussed her mother, who is now suffering from profound memory loss. “The greatest gift I have been given is playing from the Great American Songbook for my mom.” Even though she does not remember the names of the people around her, Crow said, “I can play any great song from the Great American Songbook, and she would stand up and she would sing it.” That, Crow concluded, is the power of music to outlast virtually all else.
